examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential for this patient's painful swallowing, and how you would rank it.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Given a CD4 of 64 and off ART for 8 months, my leading diagnosis is oesophageal candidiasis — supported by the oral thrush, the odynophagia, and the degree of immunosuppression. Next I'd consider CMV oesophagitis and HSV oesophagitis, both of which occur in advanced HIV but classically present with large discrete ulcers rather than diffuse plaques, and I'd only pursue these with endoscopy if he fails an empirical fluconazole trial. TB oesophagitis is rare but TB must always be screened for in HIV regardless of presenting complaint — his negative TB symptom screen and normal CXR argue against it here. Oesophageal malignancy, including Kaposi sarcoma, is less likely given his age, short symptom duration, and absence of skin lesions.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants ranked list with reasoning tied to CD4 threshold and clinical features, not just a name-drop of diagnoses.

examinerBank.question: Why do you specifically ask about CD4 count, nadir CD4, and ART history in a patient presenting with a swallowing complaint?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: CD4 count is the single most useful discriminator in HIV medicine — it predicts which opportunistic infections are likely at a given level of immunosuppression. Candida oesophagitis typically occurs once CD4 falls below 200. Nadir CD4 matters because it reflects the patient's lowest-ever immune competence and risk of latent reactivation even if current CD4 has partially recovered. ART history and adherence tell me whether the patient is virologically suppressed or at ongoing risk, and whether recent ART initiation raises concern for IRIS instead of a new opportunistic infection.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Should explicitly link CD4/nadir CD4/ART timing to the CD4-stratified differential framework, not just state 'it's important to ask'.

examinerBank.question: What is the pathophysiological mechanism behind the oral white plaques you found on examination?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Candida albicans is a normal commensal organism, but depletion of CD4 T-helper cells below approximately 200 cells/µL impairs mucosal cell-mediated immunity that normally keeps fungal proliferation in check. This allows Candida to overgrow as adherent pseudomembranous plaques composed of fungal hyphae, desquamated epithelial cells, and inflammatory debris, which is why they bleed slightly when scraped, revealing raw underlying mucosa.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Pulled directly from the pathophys pairs — wants mechanism (CD4 depletion, loss of mucosal immunity, hyphal overgrowth), not just restating 'thrush is candida'.

examinerBank.question: Why would you treat this patient empirically with fluconazole rather than proceeding straight to endoscopy?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In a resource-limited, high HIV-burden setting, the combination of odynophagia with visible oral candidiasis in a patient with a low CD4 count is considered diagnostic enough to justify an empirical trial of systemic fluconazole, which is both cheaper and less invasive than endoscopy. A clinical response within about a week confirms the diagnosis. Endoscopy with biopsy is reserved for patients who fail to respond to antifungal therapy, to look for CMV or HSV oesophagitis instead.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the empirical-trial-as-diagnostic-test concept clearly articulated, and correct identification of when endoscopy actually becomes necessary.

examinerBank.question: He was previously on ART but stopped 8 months ago. What must you check before restarting it, and why?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Before restarting or changing his ART regimen I must check his hepatitis B surface antigen status, because his regimen contains tenofovir and lamivudine, both of which have anti-HBV activity. If he is HBV-coinfected and these drugs are ever stopped or changed without care, he is at risk of a potentially fatal hepatitis flare due to rebound viral replication. I would also address his adherence barriers — his relocation and night-shift work — before simply restarting the same regimen, to try to prevent another treatment interruption.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Critical safety point emphasised in the source material — must mention HBV screening before ART changes and the flare risk, plus practical adherence planning.

patient.name: Sibusiso Ngcobo
patient.personality: stoic, downplays symptoms, embarrassed to discuss his HIV status, becomes more forthcoming once rapport is built
patient.openingLine: Doctor, it's painful when I swallow... even water burns going down.

history.fact: Pain on swallowing started about 2 weeks ago, initially mild, now severe enough that he avoids eating solid food
Describes a burning, retrosternal pain every time he swallows food or liquid, worse with solids
Also feels food getting stuck partway down, though he can still swallow liquids more easily than solids
Noticed white patches on his tongue and inside his cheeks about 3 weeks ago, which he tried to scrape off with his toothbrush
Has lost around 5 kg over the past month because eating has become so unpleasant
Appetite is reduced, not because he isn't hungry but because eating hurts
No cough, no haemoptysis, no shortness of breath
Diagnosed HIV positive 4 years ago; was on ART initially but stopped taking his tablets about 8 months ago after moving towns for work and losing his clinic file
Does not know his most recent CD4 count; last one he remembers being told, about a year ago, was 'low, around 90'
Adherence was poor even before stopping completely — often missed doses when working night shifts
No personal history of TB treatment; no known household TB contacts
No other chronic illnesses, no diabetes, no hypertension, never hospitalised before
Not currently taking any medication, including no cotrimoxazole prophylaxis (stopped along with ART)
Smokes about 5 cigarettes a day, drinks alcohol socially on weekends; lives alone in a rented room in Pinetown, works night shifts as a security guard
Has one regular partner, uses condoms inconsistently; partner's HIV status unknown to him
No family history of cancer or swallowing problems; mother has hypertension
No vomiting, no haematemesis, no abdominal pain, no diarrhoea, no headache, no visual changes, no limb weakness

examination.general: Thin, chronically unwell-looking young man. Mild pallor. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. No wasting of temporal muscles but visibly underweight. Speaks softly, occasionally winces when swallowing saliva.
examination.respiratory: Chest clear, no crackles, no dullness, normal air entry bilaterally
examination.cardio: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no elevated JVP
examination.abdo: Soft, mildly tender epigastrically on deep palpation, no hepatosplenomegaly, no masses, no ascites
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no focal deficit, no meningism, cranial nerves intact

investigations.name: HIV rapid test/ELISA (confirmatory, given lapsed care)
Empirical fluconazole trial with clinical response assessment
investigations.result: Odynophagia and oral plaques substantially improved after 5 days of oral fluconazole — supports diagnosis of candida oesophagitis without need for endoscopy

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: No infiltrate, no lymphadenopathy, no effusion

investigations.name: Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF (TB symptom screen negative but sent per protocol)
Urea & electrolytes
investigations.result: Mildly reduced sodium 132 mmol/L, otherwise normal; likely reduced oral intake

investigations.name: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy/brushings (reserved for fluconazole non-responders)
investigations.result: Not performed — clinical response to empirical antifungal therapy was diagnostic; endoscopy planned only if symptoms fail to resolve, to exclude CMV/HSV oesophagitis

against: oral candida strongly suggests fungal cause first
typically presents with large, well-circumscribed ulcers on endoscopy, not diffuse plaques
would be considered only if fluconazole trial fails
less common than candida as first presentation
would be considered on endoscopy if antifungal trial fails

differentials.dx: TB oesophagitis / mediastinal TB with oesophageal involvement
for: endemic TB, any CD4 count can be affected
against: no cough, fever, or night sweats
much rarer presentation of TB than pulmonary/lymphatic disease

differentials.dx: Oesophageal malignancy (e.g. Kaposi sarcoma or squamous cell carcinoma)
for: progressive dysphagia and weight loss can occur
against: no skin/oral KS lesions found on exam
short symptom duration and oral candida make infective cause far more likely

pathophys.odynophagia: Candida albicans overgrowth on the oesophageal mucosa in the setting of CD4-driven loss of local T-cell and mucosal immunity causes superficial ulceration and inflammation of the squamous epithelium, producing pain on the bolus passing over the inflamed mucosa
pathophys.oral thrush: Depletion of CD4 T-helper cells (normally CD4 <200 threshold) impairs mucosal cell-mediated immunity, allowing normally commensal Candida to proliferate as adherent pseudomembranous plaques of hyphae, epithelial cells and inflammatory debris
pathophys.weight loss: Reduced oral intake secondary to painful swallowing, compounded by the chronic catabolic, cytokine-driven state of untreated HIV viraemia
pathophys.progression to oesophageal (vs oral-only: Once oropharyngeal candidiasis is established, contiguous extension down the oesophageal mucosa occurs as local immune control fails further, marking WHO clinical stage 4 (AIDS-defining) disease

staging: WHO HIV clinical stage 4 (oesophageal candidiasis is AIDS-defining); CD4 64 cells/µL — advanced immunosuppression; ART-experienced but currently untreated with unsuppressed viral load

immediate: Start empirical oral fluconazole 200-400mg loading dose then 200mg daily for 14-21 days (systemic azole is first-line for oesophageal candidiasis, not topical nystatin)
Assess hydration and nutritional status; consider IV fluids if oral intake very poor
Assess swallowing safety and encourage soft/liquid diet during acute phase
definitive: Re-initiate ART (TLD — tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir) once HBsAg confirmed negative and patient counselled on adherence
Address barriers to adherence identified in history (night shift work, relocation, lost clinic file — arrange transfer of care/file retrieval)

If poor or no response to fluconazole after 7 days, refer for upper GI endoscopy with biopsy/brushings to exclude CMV/HSV oesophagitis and initiate targeted therapy (ganciclovir for CMV, aciclovir for HSV)
supportive: Nutritional support and dietary counselling; consider referral to dietician given BMI 17.5
Adherence counselling, treatment supporter, and disclosure support
TB symptom screen at every visit given ongoing risk regardless of current negative screen
followUp: Repeat CD4 and viral load at 6 and 12 months after ART restart
Monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in first 2-12 weeks after ART re-initiation
Review oral cavity and swallowing symptoms at follow-up to confirm resolution
Screen for other coinfections: repeat RPR, consider cervical/anal dysplasia screening as appropriate
Ongoing adherence support given prior treatment interruption

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, gains consent, establishes rapport given sensitive topic
stationChecklist.why: Professionalism and communication, particularly important given stigma around HIV disclosure

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the swallowing symptom — onset, whether pain (odynophagia) vs mechanical difficulty (dysphagia), solids vs liquids, progression
stationChecklist.answer: 2 weeks of burning retrosternal pain on swallowing, worse with solids, some sensation of food sticking
stationChecklist.why: Anatomically localises the problem to the oesophagus and distinguishes odynophagia (infective/inflammatory) from pure dysphagia (structural/mechanical) — the framework's core step of localising before naming a diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Specifically asks about oral symptoms — white patches, sores, taste change
stationChecklist.answer: White patches on tongue and cheeks noticed 3 weeks ago
stationChecklist.why: Oral thrush plus odynophagia is the classic clinical pairing that clinches candida oesophagitis without needing endoscopy

stationChecklist.item: Establishes HIV status, ART history, adherence, and reason for any interruption
stationChecklist.answer: Diagnosed 4 years ago, stopped ART 8 months ago after relocating for work, previously poor adherence
stationChecklist.why: Confirming HIV status and ART history is a reflex first step in any unexplained GI presentation in this setting, per framework step 1

stationChecklist.item: Asks about current/most recent CD4 count, viral load, and nadir CD4
stationChecklist.answer: Last known CD4 approx 90 a year ago, current unknown; needs repeat testing
stationChecklist.why: CD4 is repeatedly emphasised as the single most useful discriminator for CD4-stratified opportunistic disease in HIV

stationChecklist.item: Screens for TB symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss) regardless of presenting complaint
stationChecklist.answer: No cough, no fever, no night sweats — negative screen, but weight loss present from reduced intake
stationChecklist.why: TB screening is mandatory in every HIV-positive patient regardless of presenting complaint per framework step 5

stationChecklist.item: Screens weight loss, appetite, and constitutional symptoms
stationChecklist.answer: 5kg weight loss over a month due to painful eating
stationChecklist.why: Establishes severity and nutritional risk, and helps distinguish infective/constitutional causes from mechanical ones

stationChecklist.item: Performs oral cavity examination looking for thrush, hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi sarcoma
stationChecklist.answer: Confluent white plaques on tongue and buccal mucosa, adherent, bleed slightly on scraping
stationChecklist.why: Direct visualisation of oral candidiasis is the key clinical sign supporting the diagnosis without invasive testing

stationChecklist.item: Assesses general nutritional status, lymphadenopathy, skin lesions (KS), wasting
stationChecklist.answer: Thin, BMI 17.5, no lymphadenopathy, no skin lesions
stationChecklist.why: Screens for alternative/coexisting HIV-associated pathology (malignancy, disseminated disease)

stationChecklist.item: Offers ranked differential with reasoning (candida oesophagitis > CMV/HSV oesophagitis > TB oesophagitis > malignancy)
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning localised to CD4-stratified GI framework is the core exam philosophy

stationChecklist.item: Confirms HIV status, requests CD4/viral load, and justifies empirical fluconazole trial as the correct diagnostic-therapeutic approach rather than jumping straight to endoscopy
stationChecklist.answer: HIV confirmatory test, CD4 64, viral load 210,000; empirical fluconazole trial with response assessed before considering endoscopy
stationChecklist.why: Per SA/WHO guidance, empirical antifungal trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic in resource-limited settings; endoscopy reserved for non-responders

stationChecklist.item: Screens for hepatitis B before restarting/changing ART
stationChecklist.why: Her notes emphasise screening for hepatitis B before any ART change — stopping tenofovir/lamivudine in an undiagnosed HBV-coinfected patient risks a fatal flare

stationChecklist.item: Outlines fluconazole course, ART re-initiation (TLD) with adherence support, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, and TB screening continuity
stationChecklist.why: Complete, guideline-consistent management addressing both the acute OI and the underlying immunosuppression driving it
